name: Equites Stablesiani Italiciani

abilities.name: Rapid Advance
abilities.text: Improved unit movement speed over an extended period.

attributes.name: Disciplined
attributes.text: This unit does not suffer a morale penalty when the general dies. It can also rally after routing more often.

attributes.name: Hide (forest)
attributes.text: This unit can hide in forests until enemy units get too close.

attributes.name: Immune to Fear
attributes.text: This unit is immune to the fear effects of scary units.

short: The name Italiciani has a territorial origin and refers to the region where they were recruited. Stablesiani - the origin and meaning of this name remain unclear. Hoffmann suggests that these units were formed from stablemen, who, he hypothesizes, were originally attached to the new cavalry vexillations created under Gallienus. In a similar way, Speidel had previously claimed that the equites stablesiani were formed from stratores, soldiers who were attached to the personal staffs of provincial governors as stablemen or bodyguards. More recently, Speidel, rejecting this thesis, has suggested that the designation of stablesiani was originally applied to those cavalry units stationed in northwestern Italy during the reign of Gallienus under the command of Aureolus, who is identified as stabulensis, the senior officer in charge of the imperial stables. Although the origin of their title is disputed, the stablesiani appear to have been part of the comitatus (the field army accompanying the Emperor) during the military crisis of the 260-270s. Later, probably during the Tetrarchy and/or the reign of Constantine I, most of these units were permanently assigned to the garrisons of the frontier provinces. The existence of some of the equites stablesiani is testified up to the 6th century.
history: The ‘Dalmatian horsemen’ hailed from the western Balkans, roughly equivalent to the position of modern-day Croatia. Formed later in the Roman Empire as a temporary adjunct to the Legions, they became known as a ‘vexillationes’ following a reorganisation and expansion of Roman cavalry forces. In the years immediately prior the Legions had taken some heavy losses from the superior horse units of the eastern empires. This reorganisation was almost certainly an attempt to curb Roman losses and enable them to compete with the enemy's burgeoning cavalry tactics. In any case, the Dalmatae were the largest of the newly-raised vexillationes, and contributed to Claudius II victory over the Goths – a worthy record indeed!
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
